subject: Trying to estimate the stability of a variable using Lavaan.

messages.author: 54ed51586b1ca1d9
messages.subject: Trying to estimate the stability of a variable using Lavaan.
parts:
Dear colleagues,

Hope you're all doing well during this difficult year.

Disclaimer: I'm new to Lavaan and SEM, though I consider myself to be an advanced R user.

I'm trying to use a measurement model to estimate the stability of a variable across multiple measurements. . Largely, I'm trying to approximate the results obtained using a dynamic model approach. For those not familiar with it, dynamic panels are, basically, a first differences model, using the lagged levels of the variable as an instrument In a nutshell, the closer  to 0 the value of the slope, the more stable the variable is.

I seek to do a similar thing using Lavaan but I'm unsure about how to go about it–unsure about how to interpret the results or even if what I'm doing is right, even after reading the Lavaan tutorial.

Suppose I have a three wave panel, where variable x is measured at t1, t2, and t3. I simply want to get at the stability of x, for now–i.e., the simplest possible model. Here's what I have, so far:

mod <- "
  x =~ t1 + t2 + t3
"
fit <- sem(mod, data = data)

I get results, but I'm unsure about how to interpret them. What is the hypotheses being tested in the parameters?

Per reading the tutorial, I tried using labels to make t2 equal to t3, but I'm not at all sure this is what I want. I'm also unsure whether I should use growth(), rather than sem(), though they do not seem to be very different from each other.

Any help would be much appreciated.

Thank you and happy holydays to all,
-- Lucas de Abreu Maia, he/him/his
Ph.D. candidate | Department of Political Science | University of California, San Diego

messages.author: 82889e926eb5165e
messages.subject: Re: Trying to estimate the stability of a variable using Lavaan.
parts:
Lucas

This model is not evluating stability over time

mod <- "
  x =~ t1 + t2 + t3
"

This model would be testing is the three time pints consistently measure a single underlying construct X

Doing dybamic models is not straightforward in lavaan. You can only estimate them with some data managemet includedm for example with Latent Differntial Equation (LDE) with time delay embedding matrices, or estimated derivatives

Meaning the cross-lag model that you could estimate with lavaan is not a dynamic model, but a discrete time cross-lag model. The closest you could do is a latent growth curve model (which is a continuous time model), or latent change score model (simplest form of differential models).

a) If you were to estimate the cross-lag panel model, you could create a phantom factor at each time point and evaluate the stability/auto-regression between time points (lag-dependent)
b) You could also evaluate the mean differences over time with latent change score models
c) estimate a latent growth curve, estimating mean difference over time, and the variability across subjetcs
d) if you want to do dynamic models I would recommend you the ctsem or dynr R packages, which do dynamic SEM models. ctsem do dynamic continuous time models from the Exact Discrete Model approach. And dynr do dynamic continuous and discrete time models from the state space model approach

Not sure how far you have gone through the dynamic modeling literature, because I am throwing a lot of terminaology here. In case some relevant terms
- dynamic modelling
- continuous time models
- discrete time models

Depending on which approach you use, the term "stability" can mean different things. Could you explan more what do you mean by it?

Bertenthal, B. I. (2007). Dynamical Systems: It is about time! In S. M. Boker & M. J. Wenger (Eds.), Data Analytic Techniques for Dynamical Systems. Lawrence Erlbaum Associates, Inc.

messages.subject: Re: Trying to estimate the stability of a variable using Lavaan.
parts:
Dear Mauricio,

Thank you very much for such a thorough answer. 

Here's what I mean by stability of a variable: suppose I'm interested in measuring a construct such as ideology and that, in a panel survey, we ask participants about where they are placed in the ideological spectrum at T1, T2, and T3. Now, if we observe changes in that variable over time, we cannot be sure that this variation is driven by respondents truly changing their ideological self-placement or if it's driven by measurement error. So, basically, I want to distinguish true changes in a variable from measurement error.

Here are some papers that do exactly what I want to do:
  • Using dynamic panels – Schickler, E., & Green, D. P. (1997). The stability of party identification in western democracies: results from eight panel surveys. Comparative Political Studies, 30(4), 450-483. https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0010414097030004003
  • Using SEM – Prior, M. (2010). You’ve either got it or you don’t? The stability of political interest over the life cycle. The Journal of Politics, 72(3), 747-766. https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/full/10.1017/S0022381610000149?casa_token=XTEnDq0JMZgAAAAA%3APwwMXoMYu4SmFQCyaI0XySJLDucT9F7jsC3ALjyugW7-eIa8vIOw4mBN4uDi9NXcnjBh8S6J2HKG
  • Using SEM – Tucker, P. D., Montgomery, J. M., & Smith, S. S. (2019). Party Identification in the Age of Obama: Evidence on the Sources of Stability and Systematic Change in Party Identification from a Long-Term Panel Survey. Political Research Quarterly, 72(2), 309-328. https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/1065912918784215
  • Using SEM (and Lavaan, for that matter) – Kustov, A., Laaker, D., & Reller, C. (2019). The stability of immigration attitudes: Evidence and implications. Available at SSRN 3322121. https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3322121

According to your description, it seems that a) is closer to what I want, correct? Any suggestion as to how to implement it in the simple context I described in my first email?

Thanks, again,

-- Lucas de Abreu Maia, he/him/his
Ph.D. candidate | Department of Political Science | University of California, San Diego
lucasamaia.com

messages.author: 82889e926eb5165e
messages.subject: Re: Trying to estimate the stability of a variable using Lavaan.
parts:
Lucas

General comments, if you have one 1 indicator per time point the separation of real change and measurement error is limited. If you only have 3 time points, will limit the models you can estimate. Are your indicators continuous, or categorical? There seems to be variation in these papers on how the type of indicators and how to treat them. The models I suggested only applied for continuous indicators

After a quick look at some of these papers, they treat the topic of stability in very different ways. Kustov, A., Laaker, D., & Reller, C. (2019) seems to do the auto-regressive models,  Schickler, E., & Green, D. P. (1997) seems to be doing a model when they treat the indicators as dichotomous, and Tucker, P. D., Montgomery, J. M., & Smith, S. S. (2019) do an extension of the latent growth curve model. 

So,  I am not clear how you want to measure this "stability", also of your indicator is categorical, then I dont think these models would be recommended. But would suggest a Markov Model for change of category over time

I can show you syntax for some of these models, but dont want to show you syntax for a wrong model

When you say " simple context I described in my first email? ", sadly a simple contaxt doesnt provide me with enough information about what is the data like (continuous/categorical) and what is the model?

messages.subject: Re: Trying to estimate the stability of a variable using Lavaan.
parts:
I'll chime in that change in the sense of stability can be relative (position in the cohort) or absolute  (position on the scale) and these have historically often been conflated under the same label.

The autoregressive approach assesses relative stability: if the entire cohort increases by the same amount due to secular trends or some external event, that's highly stable in the relative sense even if the numbers change.

The latent growth/trajectory approach better gets at absolute stability (i.e., on the time-1 metric) by looking at both mean and variance in change over time. You'd want to see very small mean and variance of the slope to conclude absolute stability.

Pat
On Mon, Jan 4, 2021 at 11:57 AM Mauricio Garnier-Villarreal <mauga...@gmail.com> wrote:

Lucas

General comments, if you have one 1 indicator per time point the separation of real change and measurement error is limited. If you only have 3 time points, will limit the models you can estimate. Are your indicators continuous, or categorical? There seems to be variation in these papers on how the type of indicators and how to treat them. The models I suggested only applied for continuous indicators

After a quick look at some of these papers, they treat the topic of stability in very different ways. Kustov, A., Laaker, D., & Reller, C. (2019) seems to do the auto-regressive models,  Schickler, E., & Green, D. P. (1997) seems to be doing a model when they treat the indicators as dichotomous, and Tucker, P. D., Montgomery, J. M., & Smith, S. S. (2019) do an extension of the latent growth curve model. 

So,  I am not clear how you want to measure this "stability", also of your indicator is categorical, then I dont think these models would be recommended. But would suggest a Markov Model for change of category over time

I can show you syntax for some of these models, but dont want to show you syntax for a wrong model

When you say " simple context I described in my first email? ", sadly a simple contaxt doesnt provide me with enough information about what is the data like (continuous/categorical) and what is the model?



On Monday, January 4, 2021 at 5:01:02 PM UTC+1 ldea...@ucsd.edu wrote:
Dear Mauricio,

Thank you very much for such a thorough answer. 

Here's what I mean by stability of a variable: suppose I'm interested in measuring a construct such as ideology and that, in a panel survey, we ask participants about where they are placed in the ideological spectrum at T1, T2, and T3. Now, if we observe changes in that variable over time, we cannot be sure that this variation is driven by respondents truly changing their ideological self-placement or if it's driven by measurement error. So, basically, I want to distinguish true changes in a variable from measurement error.

Here are some papers that do exactly what I want to do:
  • Using dynamic panels – Schickler, E., & Green, D. P. (1997). The stability of party identification in western democracies: results from eight panel surveys. Comparative Political Studies, 30(4), 450-483. https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0010414097030004003
  • Using SEM – Prior, M. (2010). You’ve either got it or you don’t? The stability of political interest over the life cycle. The Journal of Politics, 72(3), 747-766. https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/full/10.1017/S0022381610000149?casa_token=XTEnDq0JMZgAAAAA%3APwwMXoMYu4SmFQCyaI0XySJLDucT9F7jsC3ALjyugW7-eIa8vIOw4mBN4uDi9NXcnjBh8S6J2HKG
  • Using SEM – Tucker, P. D., Montgomery, J. M., & Smith, S. S. (2019). Party Identification in the Age of Obama: Evidence on the Sources of Stability and Systematic Change in Party Identification from a Long-Term Panel Survey. Political Research Quarterly, 72(2), 309-328. https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/1065912918784215
  • Using SEM (and Lavaan, for that matter) – Kustov, A., Laaker, D., & Reller, C. (2019). The stability of immigration attitudes: Evidence and implications. Available at SSRN 3322121. https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3322121

According to your description, it seems that a) is closer to what I want, correct? Any suggestion as to how to implement it in the simple context I described in my first email?

Thanks, again,
-- Lucas de Abreu Maia, he/him/his
Ph.D. candidate | Department of Political Science | University of California, San Diego
lucasamaia.com


On Sun, Jan 3, 2021 at 7:05 PM Mauricio Garnier-Villarreal <mauga...@gmail.com> wrote:
Lucas

This model is not evluating stability over time
mod <- "
  x =~ t1 + t2 + t3
"
This model would be testing is the three time pints consistently measure a single underlying construct X

Doing dybamic models is not straightforward in lavaan. You can only estimate them with some data managemet includedm for example with Latent Differntial Equation (LDE) with time delay embedding matrices, or estimated derivatives

Meaning the cross-lag model that you could estimate with lavaan is not a dynamic model, but a discrete time cross-lag model. The closest you could do is a latent growth curve model (which is a continuous time model), or latent change score model (simplest form of differential models).

a) If you were to estimate the cross-lag panel model, you could create a phantom factor at each time point and evaluate the stability/auto-regression between time points (lag-dependent)
b) You could also evaluate the mean differences over time with latent change score models
c) estimate a latent growth curve, estimating mean difference over time, and the variability across subjetcs
d) if you want to do dynamic models I would recommend you the ctsem or dynr R packages, which do dynamic SEM models. ctsem do dynamic continuous time models from the Exact Discrete Model approach. And dynr do dynamic continuous and discrete time models from the state space model approach

Not sure how far you have gone through the dynamic modeling literature, because I am throwing a lot of terminaology here. In case some relevant terms
- dynamic modelling
- continuous time models
- discrete time models

Depending on which approach you use, the term "stability" can mean different things. Could you explan more what do you mean by it?

On Wednesday, December 30, 2020 at 5:28:17 PM UTC+1 ldea...@ucsd.edu wrote:
Dear colleagues,

Hope you're all doing well during this difficult year.

Disclaimer: I'm new to Lavaan and SEM, though I consider myself to be an advanced R user.

I'm trying to use a measurement model to estimate the stability of a variable across multiple measurements. . Largely, I'm trying to approximate the results obtained using a dynamic model approach. For those not familiar with it, dynamic panels are, basically, a first differences model, using the lagged levels of the variable as an instrument In a nutshell, the closer  to 0 the value of the slope, the more stable the variable is.

I seek to do a similar thing using Lavaan but I'm unsure about how to go about it–unsure about how to interpret the results or even if what I'm doing is right, even after reading the Lavaan tutorial.

Suppose I have a three wave panel, where variable x is measured at t1, t2, and t3. I simply want to get at the stability of x, for now–i.e., the simplest possible model. Here's what I have, so far:

mod <- "
  x =~ t1 + t2 + t3
"
fit <- sem(mod, data = data)

I get results, but I'm unsure about how to interpret them. What is the hypotheses being tested in the parameters?

Per reading the tutorial, I tried using labels to make t2 equal to t3, but I'm not at all sure this is what I want. I'm also unsure whether I should use growth(), rather than sem(), though they do not seem to be very different from each other.

Any help would be much appreciated.

Thank you and happy holydays to all,
-- Lucas de Abreu Maia, he/him/his
Ph.D. candidate | Department of Political Science | University of California, San Diego

parts:
Hi, Mauricio:

Again, thanks for helping with this and engaging with my question. You're being very generous with your time.

The variable I'm analyzing is continuous. 

Sorry, I directed you to the wrong work by Green and Schickler. I actually meant to refer to their book Partisan Hearts and Minds: https://books.google.com/books?hl=en&lr=&id=HVY18n59ThgC&oi=fnd&pg=PP9&dq=schickler+and+green+stability+partisanship&ots=cMtmaXUxmx&sig=0ydUnOXV4mfHfgEMHSSUZERdJV8#v=onepage&q=schickler%20and%20green%20stability%20partisanship&f=false. They implement an autoregressor model on a continuous variable (chapter 3). But they don't use SEM at all. They employ the Anderson and Hsiao (1981) and Arellano (1989) estimators. It's a little outdated, so that's why I wanted to implement a measurement model, as used by the more recent papers I cited in the previous email.

So, to summarize, the autoregressor model is really what I'm looking for. I understand that a three-wave panel may be too short for me to draw inferences from, but, in actuality, I'm analyzing a bunch of different panels, some of them with many more waves. I'm just starting from the simplest possible case. After that, I should be able to expand the code myself to panels with additional waves.

So, to recap, here's the data I have: a three-wave panel in which I'm interested in a continuous variable. I want to use an autoregressor model to get at how much this variable changes over time. Does that make sense?

Best wishes and thanks, again,

-- Lucas de Abreu Maia, he/him/his
Ph.D. candidate | Department of Political Science | University of California, San Diego

messages.author: 82889e926eb5165e
messages.subject: Re: Trying to estimate the stability of a variable using Lavaan.
parts:
Lucas

Ok, an autoregressor model with SEM could be done in a couple of different ways.

1. You maintain the metric and scale for the the original variable scales. This one could be done directly using the variables. With a lag 1 regression between them, we are labeling this AR1 regression a1 so that we are stating that stability effect is the same between time points
mod_reg1 <- '
t3 ~ a1*t2
t2 ~ a1*t1
'

2. You standardized the variables at each time point by creating phantom factors, and express the variance differences in the factor loadings, and mean differences in the indicator means
mod_reg2 <- '
#### phantom variables
## estimate factor loadings: standard deviations at each time point
ph_t1 =~ NA*t1
ph_t2 =~ NA*t2
ph_t3 =~ NA*t3
## fix factor variances at 1
ph_t1 ~~ 1*ph_t1
ph_t2 ~~ 1*ph_t2
ph_t3 ~~ 1*ph_t3
## fix factor means at 0
ph_t1 ~0*1
ph_t2 ~0*1
ph_t3 ~0*1
## fix indicator variances at 0. Meaning all the variance falls into the factor
t1 ~~ 0*t1
t2 ~~ 0*t2
t3 ~~ 0*t3
#### aut regression
ph_t3 ~  a1*ph_t2
ph_t2 ~  a1* ph_t1
'

3. The third options I would recommend is to use ctsem for continuous time panel models (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ctsem/index.html)


The disadvantge of 1 and 2 is that they are lag dependent, meaning that you are only presenting the auto-effect for the respective lag of time between your measurements. Option 3 allows to estimate the auto-effect independent of lag and evaluate the effect at different lags.
For example, 2 can be seen as an AR1, withount mean differences, while 1 would be cluser to ARM1, which allows for mean changes over time

I think something like this is what you are looking for?

On Mon, Jan 4, 2021 at 4:40 PM Mauricio Garnier-Villarreal <mauga...@gmail.com> wrote:

Lucas

Ok, an autoregressor model with SEM could be done in a couple of different ways.

1. You maintain the metric and scale for the the original variable scales. This one could be done directly using the variables. With a lag 1 regression between them, we are labeling this AR1 regression a1 so that we are stating that stability effect is the same between time points
mod_reg1 <- '
t3 ~ a1*t2
t2 ~ a1*t1
'

2. You standardized the variables at each time point by creating phantom factors, and express the variance differences in the factor loadings, and mean differences in the indicator means
mod_reg2 <- '
#### phantom variables
## estimate factor loadings: standard deviations at each time point
ph_t1 =~ NA*t1
ph_t2 =~ NA*t2
ph_t3 =~ NA*t3
## fix factor variances at 1
ph_t1 ~~ 1*ph_t1
ph_t2 ~~ 1*ph_t2
ph_t3 ~~ 1*ph_t3
## fix factor means at 0
ph_t1 ~0*1
ph_t2 ~0*1
ph_t3 ~0*1
## fix indicator variances at 0. Meaning all the variance falls into the factor
t1 ~~ 0*t1
t2 ~~ 0*t2
t3 ~~ 0*t3
#### aut regression
ph_t3 ~  a1*ph_t2
ph_t2 ~  a1* ph_t1
'

3. The third options I would recommend is to use ctsem for continuous time panel models (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ctsem/index.html)


The disadvantge of 1 and 2 is that they are lag dependent, meaning that you are only presenting the auto-effect for the respective lag of time between your measurements. Option 3 allows to estimate the auto-effect independent of lag and evaluate the effect at different lags.
For example, 2 can be seen as an AR1, withount mean differences, while 1 would be cluser to ARM1, which allows for mean changes over time

I think something like this is what you are looking for?

Lucas

Ok, an autoregressor model with SEM could be done in a couple of different ways.

1. You maintain the metric and scale for the the original variable scales. This one could be done directly using the variables. With a lag 1 regression between them, we are labeling this AR1 regression a1 so that we are stating that stability effect is the same between time points
mod_reg1 <- '
t3 ~ a1*t2
t2 ~ a1*t1
'

2. You standardized the variables at each time point by creating phantom factors, and express the variance differences in the factor loadings, and mean differences in the indicator means
mod_reg2 <- '
#### phantom variables
## estimate factor loadings: standard deviations at each time point
ph_t1 =~ NA*t1
ph_t2 =~ NA*t2
ph_t3 =~ NA*t3
## fix factor variances at 1
ph_t1 ~~ 1*ph_t1
ph_t2 ~~ 1*ph_t2
ph_t3 ~~ 1*ph_t3
## fix factor means at 0
ph_t1 ~0*1
ph_t2 ~0*1
ph_t3 ~0*1
## fix indicator variances at 0. Meaning all the variance falls into the factor
t1 ~~ 0*t1
t2 ~~ 0*t2
t3 ~~ 0*t3
#### aut regression
ph_t3 ~  a1*ph_t2
ph_t2 ~  a1* ph_t1
'

3. The third options I would recommend is to use ctsem for continuous time panel models (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ctsem/index.html)


The disadvantge of 1 and 2 is that they are lag dependent, meaning that you are only presenting the auto-effect for the respective lag of time between your measurements. Option 3 allows to estimate the auto-effect independent of lag and evaluate the effect at different lags.
For example, 2 can be seen as an AR1, withount mean differences, while 1 would be cluser to ARM1, which allows for mean changes over time

I think something like this is what you are looking for?

fit1 <- sem(mod_reg1, d, orthogonal = T, se="robust.huber.white", meanstructure=T)

On Mon, Jan 4, 2021 at 4:40 PM Mauricio Garnier-Villarreal <mauga...@gmail.com> wrote:
Lucas

Ok, an autoregressor model with SEM could be done in a couple of different ways.

1. You maintain the metric and scale for the the original variable scales. This one could be done directly using the variables. With a lag 1 regression between them, we are labeling this AR1 regression a1 so that we are stating that stability effect is the same between time points
mod_reg1 <- '
t3 ~ a1*t2
t2 ~ a1*t1
'

2. You standardized the variables at each time point by creating phantom factors, and express the variance differences in the factor loadings, and mean differences in the indicator means
mod_reg2 <- '
#### phantom variables
## estimate factor loadings: standard deviations at each time point
ph_t1 =~ NA*t1
ph_t2 =~ NA*t2
ph_t3 =~ NA*t3
## fix factor variances at 1
ph_t1 ~~ 1*ph_t1
ph_t2 ~~ 1*ph_t2
ph_t3 ~~ 1*ph_t3
## fix factor means at 0
ph_t1 ~0*1
ph_t2 ~0*1
ph_t3 ~0*1
## fix indicator variances at 0. Meaning all the variance falls into the factor
t1 ~~ 0*t1
t2 ~~ 0*t2
t3 ~~ 0*t3
#### aut regression
ph_t3 ~  a1*ph_t2
ph_t2 ~  a1* ph_t1
'

3. The third options I would recommend is to use ctsem for continuous time panel models (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ctsem/index.html)


The disadvantge of 1 and 2 is that they are lag dependent, meaning that you are only presenting the auto-effect for the respective lag of time between your measurements. Option 3 allows to estimate the auto-effect independent of lag and evaluate the effect at different lags.
For example, 2 can be seen as an AR1, withount mean differences, while 1 would be cluser to ARM1, which allows for mean changes over time

I think something like this is what you are looking for?

General comments, if you have one 1 indicator per time point the separation of real change and measurement error is limited. If you only have 3 time points, will limit the models you can estimate. After a quick look at some of these papers, they treat the topic of stability in very different ways. Kustov, A., Laaker, D., & Reller, C. (2019) seems to do the auto-regressive models,  Schickler, E., & Green, D. P. (1997) seems to be doing a model when they treat the indicators as dichotomous, and Tucker, P. D., Montgomery, J. So,  I am not clear how you want to measure this "stability", also of your indicator is categorical, then I dont think these models would be recommended. But would suggest a Markov Model for change of category over time

I can show you syntax for some of these models, but dont want to show you syntax for a wrong model

Lucas

This model is not evluating stability over time
mod <- "
  x =~ t1 + t2 + t3
"
This model would be testing is the three time pints consistently measure a single underlying construct X

Doing dybamic models is not straightforward in lavaan. You can only estimate them with some data managemet includedm for example with Latent Differntial Equation (LDE) with time delay embedding matrices, or estimated derivatives

Meaning the cross-lag model that you could estimate with lavaan is not a dynamic model, but a discrete time cross-lag model. The closest you could do is a latent growth curve model (which is a continuous time model), or latent change score model (simplest form of differential models).

a) If you were to estimate the cross-lag panel model, you could create a phantom factor at each time point and evaluate the stability/auto-regression between time points (lag-dependent)
b) You could also evaluate the mean differences over time with latent change score models
c) estimate a latent growth curve, estimating mean difference over time, and the variability across subjetcs
d) if you want to do dynamic models I would recommend you the ctsem or dynr R packages, which do dynamic SEM models. ctsem do dynamic continuous time models from the Exact Discrete Model approach. And dynr do dynamic continuous and discrete time models from the state space model approach

Not sure how far you have gone through the dynamic modeling literature, because I am throwing a lot of terminaology here. In case some relevant terms
- dynamic modelling
- continuous time models
- discrete time models

Depending on which approach you use, the term "stability" can mean different things. Could you explan more what do you mean by it?

Lucas

Ok, an autoregressor model with SEM could be done in a couple of different ways.

1. You maintain the metric and scale for the the original variable scales. This one could be done directly using the variables. With a lag 1 regression between them, we are labeling this AR1 regression a1 so that we are stating that stability effect is the same between time points
mod_reg1 <- '
t3 ~ a1*t2
t2 ~ a1*t1
'

2. You standardized the variables at each time point by creating phantom factors, and express the variance differences in the factor loadings, and mean differences in the indicator means
mod_reg2 <- '
#### phantom variables
## estimate factor loadings: standard deviations at each time point
ph_t1 =~ NA*t1
ph_t2 =~ NA*t2
ph_t3 =~ NA*t3
## fix factor variances at 1
ph_t1 ~~ 1*ph_t1
ph_t2 ~~ 1*ph_t2
ph_t3 ~~ 1*ph_t3
## fix factor means at 0
ph_t1 ~0*1
ph_t2 ~0*1
ph_t3 ~0*1
## fix indicator variances at 0. Meaning all the variance falls into the factor
t1 ~~ 0*t1
t2 ~~ 0*t2
t3 ~~ 0*t3
#### aut regression
ph_t3 ~  a1*ph_t2
ph_t2 ~  a1* ph_t1
'

3. The third options I would recommend is to use ctsem for continuous time panel models (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ctsem/index.html)


The disadvantge of 1 and 2 is that they are lag dependent, meaning that you are only presenting the auto-effect for the respective lag of time between your measurements. Option 3 allows to estimate the auto-effect independent of lag and evaluate the effect at different lags.
For example, 2 can be seen as an AR1, withount mean differences, while 1 would be cluser to ARM1, which allows for mean changes over time

I think something like this is what you are looking for?

This model is not evluating stability over time
mod <- "
  x =~ t1 + t2 + t3

This model would be testing is the three time pints consistently measure a single underlying construct X

Doing dybamic models is not straightforward in lavaan. You can only estimate them with some data managemet includedm for example with Latent Differntial Equation (LDE) with time delay embedding matrices, or estimated derivatives

Meaning the cross-lag model that you could estimate with lavaan is not a dynamic model, but a discrete time cross-lag model. The closest you could do is a latent growth curve model (which is a continuous time model), or latent change score model (simplest form of differential models).

a) If you were to estimate the cross-lag panel model, you could create a phantom factor at each time point and evaluate the stability/auto-regression between time points (lag-dependent)
b) You could also evaluate the mean differences over time with latent change score models
c) estimate a latent growth curve, estimating mean difference over time, and the variability across subjetcs
d) if you want to do dynamic models I would recommend you the ctsem or dynr R packages, which do dynamic SEM models. ctsem do dynamic continuous time models from the Exact Discrete Model approach. And dynr do dynamic continuous and discrete time models from the state space model approach

Not sure how far you have gone through the dynamic modeling literature, because I am throwing a lot of terminaology here. In case some relevant terms
- dynamic modelling
- continuous time models
- discrete time models

Depending on which approach you use, the term "stability" can mean different things. Could you explan more what do you mean by it?

Dear Mauricio and other colleagues who might be following this thread,

You've been extremely helpful already and I really appreciate the time you've put in helping me. But, after some simulations and reading more about AR models in lavaan, I came to the conclusion that this is not quite what I'm looking for yet. I'll explain the issue in more detail below. If you're unable to help, though, I already truly appreciate the insights you've offered so far.

As I've mentioned before, I'm trying to replicate with SEM the results I obtain with the Anderson and Hsiao (1982) and Arellano (1989) estimators. In a nutshell, their model is a first differences model within an AR framework using the initial levels of the variable of interest as an instrument. I simulated some data and ran the approaches you suggested, as well as the Anderson-Hsiao/Arellano estimator below so that you hopefully will get a better idea of what I want.

To summarize my issue, the AR model in lavaan gives me an estimate of the autoregressor. This is fine, but I'm actually interested in the autoregressor of the differences between the values of the variable at different points in time. Put differently, I want to know if previous variation in variable X predict future  variations in X. Hopefully, the code will make that clearer than I've been able to put with words.

I know that these approaches are actually very similar. Indeed, as the simulation below indicates, both retrieve the true value of the coefficients quite well. The issue is that, on the real data, I'm obtaining different substantive results with lavaan from those with the Anderson-Hsiao/Arellano estimator. That's why I want to replicate the model as closely as possible, to ensure that my results are robust.

Here are my questions: is there a way to run a first differences model in lavaan? Is the package even built to deal with these kinds of model? I also checked the ctsem package you recommended. It seems to be the right one for my purposes, but I found their vignette extremely difficult to follow. After reading it, I have no idea how to define a model in the package.

Before moving on to the code, a couple of observations about it: what I'm really interested in doing is comparing the stability of two variables. I really want to be able to say: variable X is more stable over time than variable Z. That's what the code below simulates.

Ok, an autoregressor model with SEM could be done in a couple of different ways.

1. You maintain the metric and scale for the the original variable scales. This one could be done directly using the variables. With a lag 1 regression between them, we are labeling this AR1 regression a1 so that we are stating that stability effect is the same between time points
mod_reg1 <- '
t3 ~ a1*t2
t2 ~ a1*t1
'

2. You standardized the variables at each time point by creating phantom factors, and express the variance differences in the factor loadings, and mean differences in the indicator means
mod_reg2 <- '
#### phantom variables
## estimate factor loadings: standard deviations at each time point
ph_t1 =~ NA*t1
ph_t2 =~ NA*t2
ph_t3 =~ NA*t3
## fix factor variances at 1
ph_t1 ~~ 1*ph_t1
ph_t2 ~~ 1*ph_t2
ph_t3 ~~ 1*ph_t3
## fix factor means at 0
ph_t1 ~0*1
ph_t2 ~0*1
ph_t3 ~0*1
## fix indicator variances at 0. Meaning all the variance falls into the factor
t1 ~~ 0*t1
t2 ~~ 0*t2
t3 ~~ 0*t3
#### aut regression
ph_t3 ~  a1*ph_t2
ph_t2 ~  a1* ph_t1
'

3. The third options I would recommend is to use ctsem for continuous time panel models (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ctsem/index.html)


The disadvantge of 1 and 2 is that they are lag dependent, meaning that you are only presenting the auto-effect for the respective lag of time between your measurements. Option 3 allows to estimate the auto-effect independent of lag and evaluate the effect at different lags.
For example, 2 can be seen as an AR1, withount mean differences, while 1 would be cluser to ARM1, which allows for mean changes over time

I think something like this is what you are looking for?

Doing dybamic models is not straightforward in lavaan. You can only estimate them with some data managemet includedm for example with Latent Differntial Equation (LDE) with time delay embedding matrices, or estimated derivatives

Meaning the cross-lag model that you could estimate with lavaan is not a dynamic model, but a discrete time cross-lag model. The closest you could do is a latent growth curve model (which is a continuous time model), or latent change score model (simplest form of differential models).

a) If you were to estimate the cross-lag panel model, you could create a phantom factor at each time point and evaluate the stability/auto-regression between time points (lag-dependent)
b) You could also evaluate the mean differences over time with latent change score models
c) estimate a latent growth curve, estimating mean difference over time, and the variability across subjetcs
d) if you want to do dynamic models I would recommend you the ctsem or dynr R packages, which do dynamic SEM models. ctsem do dynamic continuous time models from the Exact Discrete Model approach. And dynr do dynamic continuous and discrete time models from the state space model approach

Dear colleagues,

Hope you're all doing well during this difficult year.

Disclaimer: I'm new to Lavaan and SEM, though I consider myself to be an advanced R user.

I'm trying to use a measurement model to estimate the stability of a variable across multiple measurements. . Largely, I'm trying to approximate the results obtained using a dynamic model approach. For those not familiar with it, dynamic panels are, basically, a first differences model, using the lagged levels of the variable as an instrument In a nutshell, the closer  to 0 the value of the slope, the more stable the variable is.

I seek to do a similar thing using Lavaan but I'm unsure about how to go about it–unsure about how to interpret the results or even if what I'm doing is right, even after reading the Lavaan tutorial.

Suppose I have a three wave panel, where variable x is measured at t1, t2, and t3. I simply want to get at the stability of x, for now–i.e., the simplest possible model. Here's what I have, so far:

mod <- "
  x =~ t1 + t2 + t3
"
fit <- sem(mod, data = data)

I get results, but I'm unsure about how to interpret them. What is the hypotheses being tested in the parameters?

Per reading the tutorial, I tried using labels to make t2 equal to t3, but I'm not at all sure this is what I want. I'm also unsure whether I should use growth(), rather than sem(), though they do not seem to be very different from each other.

Any help would be much appreciated.

Thank you and happy holydays to all,
-- Lucas de Abreu Maia, he/him/his
Ph.D. candidate | Department of Political Science | University of California, San Diego
lucasamaia.com

What you describe sounds like auto-regressions between latent change scores. But when I run that model with a simulated data it does not replicate the results from ivreg(). I think the issue is what the do with | z1
What would be the equivalent use of |z1 ?

Here is an example of the auto-regression model between change scores


library(AER)
library(lavaan)
library(tidyverse)


sim_data <- tibble(
     x1 = rnorm(1000),
x2 = x1 + rnorm(1000),
x3 = x2 + rnorm(1000),
z1 = rnorm(1000),
z2 = 1.5 * z1 + rnorm(1000),
z3 = 1.5 * z2 + rnorm(1000)

)


### latent change score
### T2 - T1
### T3 - T2
change321_mod <- '
### latent true scores
PT1 =~ 1*z1
PT2 =~ 1*z2
PT3 =~ 1*z3

PT1 ~~ NA*PT1
PT2 ~~ 0*PT2
PT3 ~~ 0*PT3

PT1 ~1
PT2 ~0*1
PT3 ~0*1

z1 ~0*1
z2 ~0*1
z3 ~0*1

z1 ~~ uv*z1
z2 ~~ uv*z2
z3 ~~ uv*z3

### autoregressions
PT2 ~ 1*PT1
PT3 ~ 1*PT2

### latent change scores
change_21 =~ 1*PT2
change_32 =~ 1*PT3

change_21 ~c(m21)*1
change_32 ~c(m32)*1

### dynamic noise
change_21 ~~ c(v21)*change_21
change_32 ~~ c(v32)*change_32

### autoregressions of change scores
change_32 ~ change_21
change_21 ~ PT1
'

fit321 <- cfa(change321_mod, data=sim_data, orthogonal=T)
summary(fit321, standardized=T,rsquare=T)

Dear Mauricio and other colleagues who might be following this thread,

You've been extremely helpful already and I really appreciate the time you've put in helping me. But, after some simulations and reading more about AR models in lavaan, I came to the conclusion that this is not quite what I'm looking for yet. I'll explain the issue in more detail below. If you're unable to help, though, I already truly appreciate the insights you've offered so far.

As I've mentioned before, I'm trying to replicate with SEM the results I obtain with the Anderson and Hsiao (1982) and Arellano (1989) estimators. In a nutshell, their model is a first differences model within an AR framework using the initial levels of the variable of interest as an instrument. I simulated some data and ran the approaches you suggested, as well as the Anderson-Hsiao/Arellano estimator below so that you hopefully will get a better idea of what I want.

To summarize my issue, the AR model in lavaan gives me an estimate of the autoregressor. This is fine, but I'm actually interested in the autoregressor of the differences between the values of the variable at different points in time. Put differently, I want to know if previous variation in variable X predict future  variations in X. Hopefully, the code will make that clearer than I've been able to put with words.

I know that these approaches are actually very similar. Indeed, as the simulation below indicates, both retrieve the true value of the coefficients quite well. The issue is that, on the real data, I'm obtaining different substantive results with lavaan from those with the Anderson-Hsiao/Arellano estimator. That's why I want to replicate the model as closely as possible, to ensure that my results are robust.

Here are my questions: is there a way to run a first differences model in lavaan? Is the package even built to deal with these kinds of model? I also checked the ctsem package you recommended. It seems to be the right one for my purposes, but I found their vignette extremely difficult to follow. After reading it, I have no idea how to define a model in the package.

Before moving on to the code, a couple of observations about it: what I'm really interested in doing is comparing the stability of two variables. I really want to be able to say: variable X is more stable over time than variable Z. That's what the code below simulates.

Lucas

Ok, an autoregressor model with SEM could be done in a couple of different ways.

1. You maintain the metric and scale for the the original variable scales. This one could be done directly using the variables. With a lag 1 regression between them, we are labeling this AR1 regression a1 so that we are stating that stability effect is the same between time points
mod_reg1 <- '
t3 ~ a1*t2
t2 ~ a1*t1
'

2. You standardized the variables at each time point by creating phantom factors, and express the variance differences in the factor loadings, and mean differences in the indicator means
mod_reg2 <- '
#### phantom variables
## estimate factor loadings: standard deviations at each time point
ph_t1 =~ NA*t1
ph_t2 =~ NA*t2
ph_t3 =~ NA*t3
## fix factor variances at 1
ph_t1 ~~ 1*ph_t1
ph_t2 ~~ 1*ph_t2
ph_t3 ~~ 1*ph_t3
## fix factor means at 0
ph_t1 ~0*1
ph_t2 ~0*1
ph_t3 ~0*1
## fix indicator variances at 0. Meaning all the variance falls into the factor
t1 ~~ 0*t1
t2 ~~ 0*t2
t3 ~~ 0*t3
#### aut regression
ph_t3 ~  a1*ph_t2
ph_t2 ~  a1* ph_t1
'

3. The third options I would recommend is to use ctsem for continuous time panel models (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ctsem/index.html)


The disadvantge of 1 and 2 is that they are lag dependent, meaning that you are only presenting the auto-effect for the respective lag of time between your measurements. Option 3 allows to estimate the auto-effect independent of lag and evaluate the effect at different lags.
For example, 2 can be seen as an AR1, withount mean differences, while 1 would be cluser to ARM1, which allows for mean changes over time

I think something like this is what you are looking for?

This model is not evluating stability over time
mod <- "
  x =~ t1 + t2 + t3
"
This model would be testing is the three time pints consistently measure a single underlying construct X

Doing dybamic models is not straightforward in lavaan. You can only estimate them with some data managemet includedm for example with Latent Differntial Equation (LDE) with time delay embedding matrices, or estimated derivatives

Meaning the cross-lag model that you could estimate with lavaan is not a dynamic model, but a discrete time cross-lag model. The closest you could do is a latent growth curve model (which is a continuous time model), or latent change score model (simplest form of differential models).

a) If you were to estimate the cross-lag panel model, you could create a phantom factor at each time point and evaluate the stability/auto-regression between time points (lag-dependent)
b) You could also evaluate the mean differences over time with latent change score models
c) estimate a latent growth curve, estimating mean difference over time, and the variability across subjetcs
d) if you want to do dynamic models I would recommend you the ctsem or dynr R packages, which do dynamic SEM models. ctsem do dynamic continuous time models from the Exact Discrete Model approach. And dynr do dynamic continuous and discrete time models from the state space model approach

Not sure how far you have gone through the dynamic modeling literature, because I am throwing a lot of terminaology here. In case some relevant terms
- dynamic modelling
- continuous time models
- discrete time models

Lucas

Ok, an autoregressor model with SEM could be done in a couple of different ways.

1. You maintain the metric and scale for the the original variable scales. This one could be done directly using the variables. With a lag 1 regression between them, we are labeling this AR1 regression a1 so that we are stating that stability effect is the same between time points
mod_reg1 <- '
t3 ~ a1*t2
t2 ~ a1*t1
'

2. You standardized the variables at each time point by creating phantom factors, and express the variance differences in the factor loadings, and mean differences in the indicator means
mod_reg2 <- '
#### phantom variables
## estimate factor loadings: standard deviations at each time point
ph_t1 =~ NA*t1
ph_t2 =~ NA*t2
ph_t3 =~ NA*t3
## fix factor variances at 1
ph_t1 ~~ 1*ph_t1
ph_t2 ~~ 1*ph_t2
ph_t3 ~~ 1*ph_t3
## fix factor means at 0
ph_t1 ~0*1
ph_t2 ~0*1
ph_t3 ~0*1
## fix indicator variances at 0. Meaning all the variance falls into the factor
t1 ~~ 0*t1
t2 ~~ 0*t2
t3 ~~ 0*t3
#### aut regression
ph_t3 ~  a1*ph_t2
ph_t2 ~  a1* ph_t1
'

3. The third options I would recommend is to use ctsem for continuous time panel models (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ctsem/index.html)


The disadvantge of 1 and 2 is that they are lag dependent, meaning that you are only presenting the auto-effect for the respective lag of time between your measurements. Option 3 allows to estimate the auto-effect independent of lag and evaluate the effect at different lags.
For example, 2 can be seen as an AR1, withount mean differences, while 1 would be cluser to ARM1, which allows for mean changes over time

I think something like this is what you are looking for?

This model would be testing is the three time pints consistently measure a single underlying construct X

Doing dybamic models is not straightforward in lavaan. You can only estimate them with some data managemet includedm for example with Latent Differntial Equation (LDE) with time delay embedding matrices, or estimated derivatives

Meaning the cross-lag model that you could estimate with lavaan is not a dynamic model, but a discrete time cross-lag model. The closest you could do is a latent growth curve model (which is a continuous time model), or latent change score model (simplest form of differential models).

a) If you were to estimate the cross-lag panel model, you could create a phantom factor at each time point and evaluate the stability/auto-regression between time points (lag-dependent)
b) You could also evaluate the mean differences over time with latent change score models
c) estimate a latent growth curve, estimating mean difference over time, and the variability across subjetcs
d) if you want to do dynamic models I would recommend you the ctsem or dynr R packages, which do dynamic SEM models. ctsem do dynamic continuous time models from the Exact Discrete Model approach. And dynr do dynamic continuous and discrete time models from the state space model approach

Ok, an autoregressor model with SEM could be done in a couple of different ways.

1. You maintain the metric and scale for the the original variable scales. This one could be done directly using the variables. With a lag 1 regression between them, we are labeling this AR1 regression a1 so that we are stating that stability effect is the same between time points
mod_reg1 <- '
t3 ~ a1*t2
t2 ~ a1*t1
'

2. You standardized the variables at each time point by creating phantom factors, and express the variance differences in the factor loadings, and mean differences in the indicator means
mod_reg2 <- '
#### phantom variables
## estimate factor loadings: standard deviations at each time point
ph_t1 =~ NA*t1
ph_t2 =~ NA*t2
ph_t3 =~ NA*t3
## fix factor variances at 1
ph_t1 ~~ 1*ph_t1
ph_t2 ~~ 1*ph_t2
ph_t3 ~~ 1*ph_t3
## fix factor means at 0
ph_t1 ~0*1
ph_t2 ~0*1
ph_t3 ~0*1
## fix indicator variances at 0. Meaning all the variance falls into the factor
t1 ~~ 0*t1
t2 ~~ 0*t2
t3 ~~ 0*t3
#### aut regression
ph_t3 ~  a1*ph_t2
ph_t2 ~  a1* ph_t1
'

3. The third options I would recommend is to use ctsem for continuous time panel models (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ctsem/index.html)


The disadvantge of 1 and 2 is that they are lag dependent, meaning that you are only presenting the auto-effect for the respective lag of time between your measurements. Option 3 allows to estimate the auto-effect independent of lag and evaluate the effect at different lags.
For example, 2 can be seen as an AR1, withount mean differences, while 1 would be cluser to ARM1, which allows for mean changes over time

I think something like this is what you are looking for?

Now, if we observe changes in that variable over time, we cannot be sure that this variation is driven by respondents truly changing their ideological self-placement or if it's driven by measurement error. So, basically, I want to distinguish true changes in a variable from measurement error.

This model is not evluating stability over time
mod <- "
  x =~ t1 + t2 + t3
"
This model would be testing is the three time pints consistently measure a single underlying construct X

Doing dybamic models is not straightforward in lavaan. You can only estimate them with some data managemet includedm for example with Latent Differntial Equation (LDE) with time delay embedding matrices, or estimated derivatives

Meaning the cross-lag model that you could estimate with lavaan is not a dynamic model, but a discrete time cross-lag model. The closest you could do is a latent growth curve model (which is a continuous time model), or latent change score model (simplest form of differential models).

a) If you were to estimate the cross-lag panel model, you could create a phantom factor at each time point and evaluate the stability/auto-regression between time points (lag-dependent)
b) You could also evaluate the mean differences over time with latent change score models
c) estimate a latent growth curve, estimating mean difference over time, and the variability across subjetcs
d) if you want to do dynamic models I would recommend you the ctsem or dynr R packages, which do dynamic SEM models. ctsem do dynamic continuous time models from the Exact Discrete Model approach. And dynr do dynamic continuous and discrete time models from the state space model approach

Not sure how far you have gone through the dynamic modeling literature, because I am throwing a lot of terminaology here. In case some relevant terms
- dynamic modelling
- continuous time models
- discrete time models

Put differently, I want to know if previous variation in variable X predict future  variations in X. Hopefully, the code will make that clearer than I've been able to put with words.

I know that these approaches are actually very similar. Indeed, as the simulation below indicates, both retrieve the true value of the coefficients quite well. Ok, an autoregressor model with SEM could be done in a couple of different ways.

1. You maintain the metric and scale for the the original variable scales. This one could be done directly using the variables. With a lag 1 regression between them, we are labeling this AR1 regression a1 so that we are stating that stability effect is the same between time points
mod_reg1 <- '
t3 ~ a1*t2
t2 ~ a1*t1
'

2. You standardized the variables at each time point by creating phantom factors, and express the variance differences in the factor loadings, and mean differences in the indicator means
mod_reg2 <- '
#### phantom variables
## estimate factor loadings: standard deviations at each time point
ph_t1 =~ NA*t1
ph_t2 =~ NA*t2
ph_t3 =~ NA*t3
## fix factor variances at 1
ph_t1 ~~ 1*ph_t1
ph_t2 ~~ 1*ph_t2
ph_t3 ~~ 1*ph_t3
## fix factor means at 0
ph_t1 ~0*1
ph_t2 ~0*1
ph_t3 ~0*1
## fix indicator variances at 0. Meaning all the variance falls into the factor
t1 ~~ 0*t1
t2 ~~ 0*t2
t3 ~~ 0*t3
#### aut regression
ph_t3 ~  a1*ph_t2
ph_t2 ~  a1* ph_t1
'

3. The third options I would recommend is to use ctsem for continuous time panel models (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ctsem/index.html)


The disadvantge of 1 and 2 is that they are lag dependent, meaning that you are only presenting the auto-effect for the respective lag of time between your measurements. Option 3 allows to estimate the auto-effect independent of lag and evaluate the effect at different lags.
For example, 2 can be seen as an AR1, withount mean differences, while 1 would be cluser to ARM1, which allows for mean changes over time

I think something like this is what you are looking for?

This model would be testing is the three time pints consistently measure a single underlying construct X

Doing dybamic models is not straightforward in lavaan. You can only estimate them with some data managemet includedm for example with Latent Differntial Equation (LDE) with time delay embedding matrices, or estimated derivatives

Meaning the cross-lag model that you could estimate with lavaan is not a dynamic model, but a discrete time cross-lag model. The closest you could do is a latent growth curve model (which is a continuous time model), or latent change score model (simplest form of differential models).

a) If you were to estimate the cross-lag panel model, you could create a phantom factor at each time point and evaluate the stability/auto-regression between time points (lag-dependent)
b) You could also evaluate the mean differences over time with latent change score models
c) estimate a latent growth curve, estimating mean difference over time, and the variability across subjetcs
d) if you want to do dynamic models I would recommend you the ctsem or dynr R packages, which do dynamic SEM models. ctsem do dynamic continuous time models from the Exact Discrete Model approach. And dynr do dynamic continuous and discrete time models from the state space model approach

Not sure how far you have gone through the dynamic modeling literature, because I am throwing a lot of terminaology here. In case some relevant terms
- dynamic modelling
- continuous time models
- discrete time models

Depending on which approach you use, the term "stability" can mean different things. Could you explan more what do you mean by it?
